I know I keep saying the exact same thing over and over, and I'm sorry, I really am, it's just... it's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I'll stare at the reflective orange octagons on the sign, and it's like I'm looking at an alien artifact. I know I'm supposed to flip it, or blow my whistle, or make eye contact with the driver, but the actual sequence of what to do next is just wiped clean from my brain. 

So, maybe stress makes it worse? I don't know. All I know is that the steps I've relied on for my entire career just vanish into thin air, and I'm left standing in the middle of a live traffic lane with absolutely no thoughts in my head. That's why I'm so fixated on it. It’s just so incredibly dangerous to be this blank out there.

Well, I... I guess there is something, but I don't know if it's connected to the blankness or if it's just another part of whatever is going wrong with my head right now. It's... it's the voices. I'm not entirely sure of the exact timeline, to be honest. It's just so overwhelming to have these clear, distinct voices telling me I've done something wrong when I know I haven't, but they sound so real that I can't help but listen. And then I'm standing there with the paddle, trying to defend myself in my own mind against people who aren't even there, and the next thing I know, the steps are gone. Everything is just gone.

That is exactly what I spend hours trying to figure out, doctor. Because... well, I know I keep coming back to this exact same scenario, I know I'm repeating myself again, but it's just the only way I can make you understand how physical it all feels. It is just so incredibly confusing and exhausting to have your own senses lie to you like that, day in and day out. I'm constantly analyzing the acoustics of a voice nobody else can hear, just trying to prove to myself whether it's the environment or my own brain betraying me.

Well, doctor, that's exactly the battle I'm fighting every single day, trying to sort out what's real and what isn't, and it's just exhausting. I mean, I know I'm sounding like a broken record here, and I apologize for going on and on about the same thing, but it's just so central to my whole experience right now. It's like my brain is a scratched CD skipping on the same track. 

When you ask if they're real... well, they feel incredibly real. Like I've been saying, when the house is totally quiet, you know, when the hum of the refrigerator stops and there's just that heavy silence, or when I'm out there standing near a work zone with my stop sign and the machinery shuts off for a lunch break... that's when it happens. I hear those voices, clear as day. I mean, the tone, the pitch, the volume—it's all identical to a real person speaking. They call my name, 'Sarah,' just like that, and then they start saying I caused trouble on the block. It sounds so authentic, so physically present in the space around me, that my immediate reaction is always that it has to be real. 

But then... then I have to look at the evidence, right? Because I'll be standing there in my high-vis vest, and I'll hear them saying I caused trouble, and I'll look around at the crew. I'll look at the guy operating the backhoe, or the flagger at the other end of the zone, or just the people walking their dogs past the site. And nobody else hears them. Nobody flinches, nobody turns their head. If it were a real person shouting those things, someone would react. But it's only me. 

So, I guess... I guess deep down, in the logical part of my brain, I know they must be a product of my own mind. They have to be, if I'm the only one experiencing them. But when you're in that moment, and the silence is suddenly broken by someone calling your name and accusing you of things... it's just so hard to convince yourself it isn't real. It's a constant, draining argument I have to have with my own senses every single day.

I feel like... well, doctor, I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again, just using different words this time. Misunderstanding, misinterpretation, having doubts... it all boils down to the same thing, doesn't it? You want me to say I'm making a mistake. You want me to say I'm just confused. But I'm not.

But she isn't the one standing on the asphalt for ten hours a day, watching the same utility truck idle at the corner for no reason, listening to the police radios crackle the exact second I turn my sign. If it were just one time, or maybe twice, I could take a step back and say, 'Okay, Sarah, maybe you misunderstood that.' But it's constant. It's every single day. It's the trucks, the signs, the whispers at church, the constant feeling of being watched and evaluated... it's all of it, all connected. 

So no, I don't think it's a misunderstanding at all. I think it's exactly what it looks like. It's a massive, coordinated effort to monitor me, and it is just incredibly frustrating to have to sit here and defend my own reality when it is happening right in front of my face.

Different? No. No, why would it be different? I feel like... I feel like you're trying to find some sort of gap, like some crack in the foundation of my mind where things get lost in translation, but there isn't one. 

When I am standing out there on the asphalt, holding my stop paddle, and I see the white utility truck pull up to the corner of 4th and Elm, I think to myself, "That truck has been idling for twelve minutes, and the driver hasn't looked at his phone once, he's just watching the pilot car." That is exactly what I think in my head. And then, when I go home and try to explain it to my sister Sarah, I say, "Sarah, the white truck idled for twelve minutes and the driver just watched the pilot car." It is exactly the same. It's a one-to-one ratio. 

The way the connections form in my head—like noticing that the static on the police scanner always flares up in that specific rhythm right when I flip my sign—that exact same sequence is what comes out of my mouth. I don't filter it. I don't change it to make it sound prettier or simpler, because if I simplify it, it loses the truth of what's actually happening. I just try to give you, or Sarah, or anyone who will actually listen for two seconds, the exact blueprint of what is happening in my brain. Because if I leave out even a single detail, if I don't explain it exactly how I am experiencing it, you won't see the pattern. You won't realize that the paving crew's schedule shifted on the exact same day the whispers at church started getting louder. 

So, no, my explaining isn't different from my thinking. My words are a perfect mirror of my thoughts. I just... I really need you to understand that I am not confused about what I'm saying. I am just thorough. I have to be thorough, because the people monitoring me are thorough, and if I don't explain every single piece of the puzzle exactly how I see it in my mind, no one is ever going to believe me.
